lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Opposite charges attract each other.
  • An object that is negatively charged has gained electrons.
  • Static electricity means an imbalance of electrons.
  • A glass rod becomes positively charged when rubbed with silk.
  • An ebonite rod and a glass rod brought together after being rubbed with fur attract each other.
  • A person who gains a positive charge on a carpet feels a shock when electrons flow from a neutral doorknob to the hand.
  • Lightning hits buildings and homes because they are the closest point to thunder clouds.
  • An electrostatic precipitator is used in pollution control.
  • Like charges repel each other while opposite charges attract each other.
  • The path on which current flows is called a circuit.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Select the correct answers for the following questions

Q: 1. Opposite charges __________ each other.

Options: (a) Attract (b) Repel (c) Cancel (d) None of them

Correct answer: Attract

Q: 2. An object that is negatively charged has:

Options: (a) gained protons (b) lost protons (c) gained electrons (d) lost electrons

Correct answer: gained electrons

Q: 3. The term "electricity" in referring to static electricity, Means:

Options: (a) An imbalance of protons (b) An equal number of atoms (c) An imbalance of electrons (d) An imbalance of neutrons

Correct answer: An imbalance of electrons

Q: 4. Which one rod will become positively charged when rubbed with silk:

Options: (a) Glass rod (b) Carbon rod (c) Silver rod (d) Ebonite rod

Correct answer: Glass rod

Q: 5. If an ebonite rod and a glass rod are brought together after being rubbed with fur, which of the following will happen?

Options: (a) They will remain stationery (b) They will attract each other (c) They will repel each other (d) None of them

Correct answer: They will attract each other

Q: 6. You are walking on a carpet and gain a positive charge. When you touch a neutral doorknob:

Options: (a) The electrons flow from the doorknob to your hand and you feel a shock. (b) The electrons flow from your hand to the doorknob and you feel a shock (c) The electrons do not flow and you feel no shock. (d) The electrons do not flow but you still feel a shock.

Correct answer: The electrons flow from the doorknob to your hand and you feel a shock.

Q: 7. Why does lightning hit buildings and homes?

Options: (a) They are the closest point to thunder clouds. (b) They are good insulators. (c) Lightning clouds tend to form over buildings. (d) None of these.

Correct answer: They are the closest point to thunder clouds.

Q: 8. Electrostatic precipitator is used.

Options: (a) In pollution control (b) In electro painting (c) In automobiles (d) To protect from lightening

Correct answer: In pollution control

Q: 9. Which one phenomenon is not related to static electricity?

Options: (a) Both unlike and like charges attract (b) Like charges repel (c) Opposite charges attract (d) Neutral objects are attracted to charged objects

Correct answer: Both unlike and like charges attract

Q: 10. The path on which current flow is called __________.

Options: (a) Resistance (b) Resistor (c) Circuit (d) none of these.

Correct answer: Circuit

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A metallic chain hanging from a petrol tanker touches the ground and provides a conducting path so static charges flow to the ground instead of accumulating and causing fire or explosion.
  • Electrostatic induction is the redistribution of charges on a neutral conducting body due to a nearby charged body without any physical contact.
  • A fuse is a thin metallic wire of low melting point connected in the live wire in series, and it melts and breaks the circuit when the current exceeds the limit.
  • A closed circuit has a complete path and current flows in it, while an open circuit has no complete path and no current flows.
  • A circuit breaker is a switch that automatically turns off the circuit when current exceeds the specified value and can be reset and used again.
  • Current electricity is produced by the flow of charges through a conductor and is of two types, direct current and alternating current.
  • Hair stands on ends after removing a cap because electrons transfer from the cap to the hair and hairs with the same charge repel each other.
  • A lightning rod protects a building because lightning follows the shortest way to the ground through the rod and its grounded wire.
  • Static charges are called static because they are confined to the rubbed areas of objects and are unable to move to other areas.
  • Polarization of charge shifts the centres of positive and negative charge in a molecule slightly, producing an induced charge on the surface of an insulator.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Write short answers of the following questions

Q: 1. Why a metallic chain is hanging from the rear side of a petrol supply tanker.

Ans: Static charges are built up on the body of the vehicle due to friction, and in vehicles carrying inflammable material like petrol this large charge can cause fire and explosion. The hanging metallic chain touches the ground and provides a conducting path for the flow of static charges towards the ground. In this way it prevents the accumulation of static charges on the body of the tanker.

Q: 2. Define electrostatic induction.

Ans: Electrostatic induction is the redistribution of charges on the surface or inside a neutral conducting body due to the presence of a charged body in its proximity, without any physical contact. The side of the uncharged body close to the charged body becomes oppositely charged, while its other side gains a similar charge to that of the charged body, and this redistribution lasts only while the charged body is kept nearby. Diagram (in words): Fig. 6.2 Electrostatic induction shows a negatively charged ebonite rod held near a metallic rod on an insulated stand, with positive charge marked at end A near the rod and negative charge marked at the far end B.

Q: 3. Describe fuse and its importance.

Ans: A fuse is a thin and small piece of metallic wire of low melting point, connected in the live wire, often as a cartridge, and in series along the main supply line so that the entire current passes through it. If a fault develops and the current exceeds the limits, the fuse overheats and melts, thereby breaking the circuit before the circuit catches fire. Its importance is that it protects the wiring and appliances from damage due to excessive current.

Q: 4. What is meant by circuit, closed circuit and open circuit?

Ans: The path for the flow of electric current is called an electric circuit. When the switch is on and current flows in the circuit, it is called a closed circuit, because it has a complete path for current flow. When the switch is off or the power supply is disconnected and no current flows in the circuit, it is called an open circuit, because it does not have a complete path for current flow. Diagram (in words): Fig. 6.9 Different types of circuits shows a Close circuit on the left, with a battery and a glowing bulb joined in a complete loop, and an Open circuit on the right, with the bulb unlit and one wire disconnected.

Q: 5. What is a circuit breaker? Describe its importance.

Ans: A circuit breaker is a modified form of fuse, in the form of a switch that automatically turns off the circuit when the current exceeds the specified value. Unlike a fuse, it does not melt, and it can be reset by turning the switch on or by pressing a button. Its importance is that it protects the circuit and appliances from excessive current and can be used again and again after a fault.

Q: 6. What is meant by current electricity? Describe its types.

Ans: Electricity which is produced due to the flow of charges (electrons or ions) through conducting material is called current electricity or electric current. It is of two types: direct current (DC), which flows in one direction only, and alternating current (AC), which regularly changes its direction. The alternating current supplied to our homes changes its direction 100 times in one second.

Q: 7. Why do your hair stand on ends when you pull apart your cap?

Ans: When you pull apart the cap from your hair, electrons are transferred from the cap to the hair. As all the hairs acquire the same charge, they repel each other and tend to get away from each other as much as possible. This is the reason for the hair raising phenomenon, in which the hair stand on ends.

Q: 8. How does a lightning rod protect a building from a lightning strike?

Ans: A lightning rod is a metal rod attached to the roof of a house or a building, and its lower end is connected to a copper or aluminum wire which goes down to the earth and is grounded. Lightning always follows the shortest way to the ground, so if it strikes the lightning rod on a building, it goes down along the wire to the earth. Thus the lightning rod protects the building from the hazard of lightning. Diagram (in words): Fig. 6.7 Lightning Rod shows a building with a vertical rod on its roof labelled Lighting rod, a wire running down the side of the building, and Ground terminals spread in the earth below.

Q: 9. Define static charges. Why are they called static?

Ans: The charges produced on objects by rubbing them together, or by pressing and pulling them apart, are called static charges. They are called static because these charges are confined to the rubbed areas of the objects and are unable to move to other areas of the same objects. An object becomes negatively charged if it gains electrons and positively charged if it loses electrons, so a static charge is an imbalance between negative and positive charges.

Q: 10. What is meant by polarization of charge?

Ans: In most neutral atoms or molecules, the center of positive charge coincides with the center of negative charge, but in the presence of a charged object these centers may shift slightly, resulting in positive charge on one side of the molecule and negative charge on the other side. This effect is known as polarization of charge. Polarization of charges within individual molecules produces an induced charge on the surface of an insulator, and this effect explains why a comb that has been moved through hair attracts bits of neutral paper.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Electric charge is always conserved because rubbing only transfers electrons from one body to the other and never creates charge.
  • The force of attraction or repulsion between charged bodies is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
  • An electrostatic spark is produced when electrons jump the gap between highly charged bodies and heat the air until it glows.
  • In a series circuit there is only one path for current and the total resistance is equal to the sum of the resistances of all the resistors.
  • In a parallel circuit the voltage across each resistor is equal to the circuit voltage, so house appliances keep working if one of them stops.
  • In electrostatic painting, positively charged paint particles are attracted to an earthed metallic body and form a uniform coat of paint on its surface.
  • An electrostatic precipitator gives smoke and dust particles a static charge and collects them on a plate of opposite charge, thereby reducing air pollution.
  • In a bulb, electric current passing through the filament is converted into heat and light energies.
  • Electrical equipment should never be used in or close to water as one of the safety measures against the hazards of electricity.
  • A solar panel is formed by connecting a number of solar cells in series to generate a large amount of voltage.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Write detail answers of the following questions

Q: 1. What are the basic characteristics of static charges?

Ans: The basic characteristics of static charges given in this unit are as follows. (i) Conservation of charges: Ordinarily objects are electrically neutral and contain equal numbers of electrons and protons, and when one body is rubbed against another, charge is not created; the electrified state is due to transfer of electrons from one body to the other, so one body gains some amount of negative charge while the other gains an equal amount of positive charge, and electric charge is always conserved - for example, when a glass rod is rubbed with silk, the silk obtains a negative charge equal in magnitude to the positive charge on the glass rod. (ii) Attraction: Static charges make certain materials attract each other - a glass rod rubbed with silk cloth or an ebonite rod rubbed with a woolen cloth develops static charge and can attract small particles, and a plastic comb moved in dry hair gathers static charges and starts attracting small pieces of paper. (iii) Repulsion: Static charges also produce repulsion, because like charges repel each other - when hair is combed on a dry day, negative charge builds up on the comb and positive charge on the hair, and as all the hair acquire the same charge they repel each other, causing the flyaway of hair. (iv) The force of attraction or repulsion between charged bodies is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

Q: 2. Describe the effects of static charges.

Ans: Two effects of static charges are described in this unit. (i) Electrostatic sparks: A spark is produced due to heating up of air present between two highly charged bodies. If there are more positive charges on one object and equally negative charges on the surface of another object, the attraction between the charges may be great enough to make the electrons jump the gap between the highly charged objects; once a few electrons start to move across the gap they heat up the air, more electrons jump across quickly, and the air gets so hot that for a very short period of time it glows and produces a spark, known as an electrostatic spark. The same phenomenon is seen during thunderstorms, when electrostatic sparks are produced on a much larger scale, resulting in lightning. (ii) Polarization charges: In most neutral atoms or molecules the center of positive charge coincides with the center of negative charge, but in the presence of a charged object these centers may shift slightly, resulting in positive charge on one side of the molecule and negative charge on the other side; this effect is called polarization, and it produces an induced charge on the surface of an insulator, which is why a comb moved through hair attracts bits of neutral paper.

Q: 3. What is meant by resistance? How resistors are connected in a circuit?

Ans: The opposition offered by a conductor to the flow of electric current is called its resistance, while the conductor is called a resistor. The electrical appliances connected in a circuit act as resistors, and the basic function of a resistor is to control the magnitude of current flowing in a circuit. Resistors in a circuit can be connected in two ways. (a) In series: In a series circuit there is only one path for the flow of current and the same amount of current flows through all the resistors; the total voltage across the circuit is equal to the sum of the voltages across all the resistors, and the total resistance is equal to the sum of the resistances of all the resistors - an example is a string of decoration lights, where if any one bulb is missing or burnt out, no current will flow and none of the lights will work. (b) In parallel: In a parallel circuit there are two or more paths for the flow of current and different amounts of current flow through each resistor, while the voltage of the circuit is equal to the voltage across each resistor - an example is the wiring system of a house, where if one appliance stops working, current still flows through the other appliances. Diagram (in words): Fig. 6.10 Series circuit shows three loads in a single loop labelled Load on circuit, joined to a Voltage pump, with the Current shown flowing in one path, while Fig. 6.11 Parallel circuit shows the loads joined in separate branches to the same supply.

Q: 4. Describe the practical applications of static electricity.

Ans: Static electricity has many applications, for example in photocopiers, inkjet printers, laser printers, high voltage generators, electrostatic painting and electrostatic precipitators, and the unit also describes its use in smokestacks and air fresheners. (i) Electrostatic or electro painting: This principle is applied to paint uniformly the surfaces of metallic bodies such as refrigerators, metallic furniture, metallic boxes and automobiles; the surface of the metallic body is earthed, the paint particles emerging from the nozzle of the spray machine acquire positive charge due to friction, and when these positively charged particles come near the metallic body they induce negative charge on it, so due to the force of attraction between opposite charges a uniform coat of paint is formed on the surface. (ii) Electrostatic precipitators for pollution control: An electrostatic precipitator removes unwanted solid or liquid particles from gases; large precipitators are used in coal-burning power plants and industrial plants that generate large quantities of smoke, where a static charge (usually positive) is produced on smoke, dust and other unwanted particles passing through, and these charged particles are attracted by a plate having opposite charge, collected and finally removed, thereby reducing air pollution, while small precipitators are used in homes with heating and cooling systems. In smokestacks, positive charge is induced on smoke and dust particles by a positively charged wire gauze, and negatively charged plates attract and deposit them, so the outgoing gases are cleaned. An air freshener or air ionizer works on the same principle: it strips off electrons from smoke, dust and pollen particles so they gain positive charge and are deposited on a negatively charged plate, freshening and purifying the air.

Q: 5. Write about practical uses of current electricity in household appliances?

Ans: Most practical applications of electricity deal with current electricity, and at home electric current is converted into other forms of energy according to the need, for lighting, heating, cooling, washing and other purposes. For lighting, when electric current passes through the filament of a bulb it heats up so much that it emits light, so electric current is converted into heat and light energies. For heating, the electric room heater, electric iron, immersion rod and electric kettle contain high resistance metallic heating coils, and when these appliances are switched on the electric current is converted into heat energy in these coils; in the clothes drier machine, hair drier, toaster and oven, electric current is converted into heat and mechanical energy. For cooling, in the electric fan, air cooler and air conditioner used in summer, the blades start rotating when electric current flows, so electric current is converted into mechanical energy. Similarly, in the washing machine and electric motor, electric current is converted into mechanical energy, and other household appliances like the refrigerator, television and computer need electric current for their operation. In other words, current electricity has become a necessity of our life.

Q: 6. What safety measures should be adopted to avoid hazards of electricity?

Ans: To avoid the hazards of electricity in homes and in our surroundings, the following safety measures given in this unit should be adopted: (1) Do not touch switches unnecessarily. (2) Never use electrical equipment in or close to water. (3) Never play near broken plugs or in areas with many electrical wires and appliances. (4) Never pull out a plug by pulling its cable. (5) Never touch any torn or taped cables or switches, and keep them away from heat and water. (6) Avoid touching electrical appliances with any metallic object. (7) Never go near a declined (fallen) power line. (8) Avoid climbing electric poles, transmission towers or fences around power stations. (9) Avoid climbing trees or poles that are near power lines. (10) Always contact an electrician or relevant expert in case of any fault in a circuit or in an electrical appliance.

Q: 7. Write a note on energy generation from renewable resources.

Ans: Energy resources which do not deplete on consumption are called renewable energy resources, such as sunlight, wind, flowing water, rain, tides, waves, biomass and geothermal heat. They are needed because a large amount of energy in the world is obtained from coal, petroleum products and natural gas, which are not renewable, are gradually decreasing and will ultimately be depleted, and are also not environment friendly, causing global warming and ozone layer depletion. (1) Sunlight: Solar energy is the large amount of energy received from sunlight in the form of light and heat; a solar cell is a device that directly converts solar energy into electric energy, a single solar cell produces a small voltage, and a number of solar cells connected in series to generate a large amount of voltage form a solar panel - solar panels are used in offices and homes during load shedding, in artificial satellites, in agriculture, and to operate tube wells where conventional electric facility is not available. (2) Flowing water: Flowing water is a useful renewable resource of hydro energy; water is stored in dams and passed through tunnels where it turns huge turbines whose rotating shafts are connected to generators that generate electricity, which is then supplied to homes, offices and industries through cables. (3) Wind: Wind blows from regions of high pressure towards regions of low pressure; wind mills convert wind energy into mechanical energy for operating tube wells and flour mills, and nowadays wind energy is used for operating turbines which generate electricity - in Pakistan it can be utilized in coastal areas and high mountainous areas like Chitral, Gilgit and Swat. (4) Biomass: Biomass consists of organic materials like animal manure, sawdust of timber mills, plant and tree residues, crop residue and used tires; energy is obtained from it by direct burning, in which the solid waste is fed into a furnace producing heat used to boil water and run turbines and generators for generating electric energy, or by fermentation, in which biomass enclosed in a tank is decomposed by bacterial action to produce methane gas, which is then utilized for different energy purposes.

Key Points

  • A chemical reaction can be shown by a change in state, evolution of a gas, or a change in color.
  • Rust is iron oxide.
  • In glucose metabolism, pyruvate molecules may be fermented into lactic acid.
  • A chemical reaction involves both the breaking of bonds and the formation of bonds.
  • Melting of ice is not a chemical change.
  • The formation of water needs hydrogen, oxygen and a spark.
  • Retreading is used for the recycling of tyres.
  • The chemical name of Vitamin C is ascorbic acid.

Q: 2. How iron get rusted?

Ans: A layer of rust forms over unpainted iron surfaces and gradually leads to the disintegration of the iron. In the rusting process iron combines with oxygen in the presence of atmospheric moisture, resulting in the formation of iron oxide (Fe2O3), which is rust. The reaction is: 4Fe + 3O2 + xH2O -> 2Fe2O3.xH2O (Iron + Oxygen + Moisture -> Rust).

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Scientific nomenclature is the naming of chemical compounds, whose scientific names are based upon their chemical structure.
  • Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long chain fatty acids such as stearic, oleic or palmitic acid.
  • In soap preparation, the heat of steam first melts the fat and sodium hydroxide then combines with the fat or oil to form soap along with glycerin.
  • Sodium chloride is added to the soap mixture to separate the glycerin, which settles at the bottom while the soap floats at the surface.
  • In photosynthesis, green plants convert water and carbon dioxide into glucose and oxygen with chlorophyll trapping energy from sunlight.
  • Burning of coal and natural gas involves carbon and methane reacting with oxygen in combustion to release energy for domestic and industrial use.
  • The three methods of chemical disposal are reducing the use of hazardous materials, reuse and recycle, and disposal of wastes in land based disposal areas.
  • Retreading old tyres produces functional tyres that can be used again, and recovered rubber can cost half that of natural or synthetic rubber.
  • Chemical waste is regarded as hazardous waste if it is ignitable, corrosive, reactive and toxic.
  • In Pakistan, hazardous wastes are often released by contractors into nearby water bodies, residential areas or cultivable lands, from where they make their way into the food chain.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Write detailed answers of the following questions

Q: 1. What do you mean by the term scientific nomenclature? Explain it with examples.

Ans: Scientific nomenclature (chemical nomenclature) is the term given to the naming of chemical compounds. Different chemical compounds have scientific names based upon their chemical structure, and these names are often complicated and long, understandable only to those who have background knowledge of chemistry, while commonly used compounds may have several names. For example, baking soda is a white substance available in powder form and used in every kitchen, and its chemical name is sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3). Other examples from the chapter are: Vinegar — Acetic acid; Vitamin C — Ascorbic acid; Vitamin B9 — Folic acid; Vitamin D — Ergocalciferol; Aspirin — Acetylsalicylic acid; and Margarine — Partially saturated fatty acid. Generally chemists use common chemical names more when mentioning ingredients in everyday consumer products, and food and cosmetic labels use these names to inform consumers about the ingredients present in a product.

Q: 2. How soap is prepared from oil and sodium hydroxide?

Ans: Soaps are chemically sodium or potassium salts of long chain fatty acids, such as stearic, oleic or palmitic acid, which are present in vegetable oils or animal fats. The mixture of fat or vegetable oil and caustic soda (NaOH) is put in a steel tank fitted with steam coils, with an outlet at the bottom, and steam is passed through the mixture. The heat of the steam first melts the fat, and sodium hydroxide then combines with the fat or oil to form soap along with glycerin; this process is called saponification. To separate the glycerin, sodium chloride is added to the soap mixture: glycerin dissolves in the sodium chloride solution and, being heavier than the soap, settles at the bottom, while the soap floats at the surface, so the glycerin solution is removed by opening the tap at the bottom of the tank. Soap produced for commercial purposes also contains synthetic lathering agents, artificial colors and a range of chemicals. Diagram (in words): The figure labelled 'Soap preparation tank' shows Vegetable oil and Sodium hydroxide entering the Iron tank from the top, Steam entering through coils on the side, a layer of Soap above the Glycerin inside the tank, and an outlet tap at the bottom.

Q: 3. Relate chemical reactions to familiar processes encountered in everyday life.

Ans: Many familiar everyday processes are chemical reactions. (1) Photosynthesis: green plants manufacture their own food, converting water and carbon dioxide into glucose and oxygen with chlorophyll trapping energy from sunlight: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2. (2) Rusting of iron: iron combines with oxygen in the presence of atmospheric moisture to form iron oxide (rust): 4Fe + 3O2 + xH2O -> 2Fe2O3.xH2O. (3) Burning of coal and natural gas: carbon and methane react with oxygen in combustion to release energy for domestic and industrial use: C + O2 -> CO2 + Energy and CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + Energy. (4) Everyday products such as toothpaste, soap, shampoo and washing powder are all results of chemical reactions. (5) Technological processes include film processing, where light acts on silver bromide crystals to form a latent image that is developed and fixed with sodium thiosulfate; food processing, including fermentation; fabric and hair dyeing, where the dye forms chemical bonds with the fabric; agriculture, where nitrogen-fixing bacteria make nitrogen available to plants; pulp-and-paper making, where wood pieces are treated with NaOH and Na2S to remove lignin; and mineral processing, such as making Plaster of Paris from gypsum and chlorine and sodium hydroxide by electrolysis of sodium chloride solution. Diagram (in words): The figure labelled 'Photosynthesis' shows Light Energy from the sun and Carbon dioxide entering the leaves of a flowering plant, Water taken up from the soil by its roots, and Oxygen being released from the leaves.

Q: 4. List the methods of chemical disposal and briefly describe each method.

Ans: The chapter lists three effective disposal methods for hazardous wastes. (1) Reducing the use of hazardous materials: one option for minimizing the generation of hazardous waste is to minimize its consumption in different chemical industries, which in turn generates a smaller amount of hazardous waste. (2) Reuse and recycle: hazardous wastes are reused and recycled if possible, that is, materials are used again in their original or changed forms rather than thrown away as waste, which ensures safe disposal and is cost effective; for example, acetone can be recovered from spent solvents and hydraulic fluids and used oils can be recovered from automobiles, lead-acid batteries are recycled and reused in cars and other automobiles, rubber and tyres are reclaimed and retreaded, plastics are separated at recycling centres and remade into daily-use items, and metals such as aluminium, tin and steel are collected and processed through recycling units for use again without compromising quality and strength. (3) Disposal of wastes in land based disposal areas: hazardous wastes are thrown in a landfill, waste pile, injection well or other land based disposal area, but this method must be supported by proper precautions and necessary regulations so that people living adjacent to it, and the environment and natural resources of that locality, remain safe and protected.

Q: 5. Describe how old tyres can be recycled and reused.

Ans: Tyres are one of the serious issues where rubber waste in landfill is concerned. At the international level rubber tyres are disposed of by incineration, retreading, recycling or simply throwing them in landfill. One of the better options for tyre recycling is retreading, in which old tyres produce functional tyres that can be used again. More generally, when rubber is reclaimed and recycled, less energy is used than in producing new rubber; recovered rubber can cost half that of natural or synthetic rubber, and the recovered rubber has some properties that are better than those of fresh rubber. At the same time, recycling rubber saves the rubber tree plantations too.

Q: 6. Explain the impacts and safety consequences of chemical disposal in Pakistan.

Ans: Chemical waste is regarded as hazardous waste if it is ignitable, corrosive, reactive and toxic, and it is a serious threat to human health and the environment if it is not properly managed or disposed of. In Pakistan there is no proper mechanism and infrastructure for the disposal of chemical wastes, and the facilities for treatment, recycling and waste disposal are still in the developmental stage. In most cases hazardous wastes produced by the chemical industries are given to contractors who are least bothered about safety precautions, and they often release the wastes into nearby water bodies, residential areas or cultivable lands, from where the wastes make their way into the food chain. Similarly, chemicals used in tanneries and textile industries, including bleaching agents, toxic and inflammable solvents, acids and alkalis, are often discharged untreated into nearby water bodies or open land, and people living in such localities become victims of several dangerous diseases including cancer. Improper disposal also creates different types of pollution, and improper storage and management of chemical wastes and accidents during the transport and distribution of chemicals affect particular ecosystems, while the unmanaged use of fertilizers, pesticides, insecticides and herbicides in agriculture produces further health and environmental concerns, so proper planning must be done for the safe disposal of these harmful wastes.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Nuclear pores provide a passage for the exchange of proteins and ribonucleic acids between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
  • The nucleus stores hereditary material in the form of genes and also stores different types of proteins and RNA in the nucleolus.
  • Messenger RNA carries information from DNA, transfer RNA transports amino acids, and ribosomal RNA helps translate messenger RNA into peptides.
  • The four nitrogenous bases in DNA are adenine, guanine, thymine and cytosine, with adenine pairing with thymine and guanine pairing with cytosine.
  • Interphase is the resting phase between two mitotic divisions during which the nucleus prepares itself for division.
  • Mitosis supports growth, keeps the number of chromosomes constant, transmits hereditary characters equally, helps in the healing of wounds and forms new cells.
  • Genetic disorders are transmitted from parents to offspring and arise from defects in a gene or an abnormal number of chromosomes.
  • The transfer of genetic information from DNA to messenger RNA and then to the cytoplasm takes place in the two steps of transcription and translation.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Write short answers of the following questions

Q: 1. What is the role of nuclear pores in the nucleus?

Ans: The nuclear membrane has several openings called nuclear pores. These pores provide a passage for the exchange of materials like different types of proteins and ribonucleic acids between the nucleus and the cytoplasm. In this way the nucleus communicates with the remaining part of the cell or the cytoplasm through the nuclear pores.

Q: 2. List down four major functions of nucleus.

Ans: Four major functions of the nucleus are: (1) The nucleus is the site of storage of hereditary material in the form of genes, and it also stores different types of proteins and RNA in the nucleolus. (2) Messenger RNA (mRNA) and ribosomes are formed in the nucleus, which are responsible for protein synthesis. (3) It is a site for the exchange of hereditary molecules (DNA and RNA) between the nucleus and the rest of the cell. (4) When the cell divides, the chromatin network breaks into chromosomes, which are then equally transmitted into the offsprings.

Q: 3. Write the role of RNA as a carrier of information?

Ans: DNA is not directly involved in protein synthesis; it is the storehouse of genetic information, and that information is transferred to RNA. Messenger RNA (mRNA) carries the information from the DNA, according to which protein is synthesized, while transfer RNA (tRNA) carries out the transport of amino acids to the site of protein synthesis. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) in the ribosome cooperates with tRNAs to translate mRNAs into peptides, so the transfer of genetic information from DNA to mRNA and then to the cytoplasm takes place in two steps, transcription and translation.

Q: 4. Name the four types of nitrogenous bases found in the DNA molecule.

Ans: The four types of nitrogenous bases found in the DNA molecule are adenine, guanine, thymine and cytosine. In the DNA molecule adenine always pairs with thymine and guanine always pairs with cytosine, so DNA has equal numbers of adenine and thymine (A=T) and equal numbers of guanine and cytosine (C=G).

Q: 5. Define interphase.

Ans: The resting phase between any two mitotic divisions is called interphase. During this phase the nucleus and cytoplasm become active and the nucleus prepares itself for division. The daughter cells formed after division also pass into interphase, during which they grow to their normal size.

Q: 6. Briefly write about the significance of mitosis.

Ans: Mitosis plays an important role in the growth of an organism and keeps the number of chromosomes constant. By mitosis the hereditary characters are equally transmitted into the daughter cells, because each daughter cell receives exactly the same number and the same kind of chromosomes as the parent cell. It also helps in the healing of wounds and in the formation of new cells.

Q: 7. What do you mean by genetic disorders?

Ans: Genetic disorders, or genetic diseases, are those disorders which are transmitted from parents to the offsprings. They arise from defects or changes in the hereditary material, for example a defect in a gene or an abnormal number of chromosomes. Thalassemia and Down's syndrome, discussed in this unit, are common examples of genetic disorders.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The nucleus is separated from the cytoplasm by a double-layered nuclear membrane and contains nucleoplasm, a nucleolus and chromosomes.
  • Chromosome numbers are specific to each species, such as 46 in man, 26 in frog, 14 in pea and 48 in potato.
  • A nucleotide is composed of a 5-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogen-containing base.
  • A chromosome is composed of DNA and a protein called histone and carries genetic information in the form of genes.
  • In the Watson and Crick model, the sugar-phosphate chain is located on the outer side of DNA while the nitrogenous bases project towards the centre.
  • DNA replication produces two identical double-stranded DNA molecules from one original molecule, with each old strand acting as a pattern for a new complementary strand.
  • Meiosis produces four haploid daughter cells and causes exchange of genes, so genetic variation occurs among the species.
  • Down's syndrome is caused by an extra chromosome 21, making the total chromosome number 47 instead of 46.
  • Transgenic plants carry introduced genes for resisting infections and attacking insects, making biotech crops more profitable and productive.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Write detail answers of the following questions

Q: 1. Describe the structure and function of nucleus.

Ans: Structure: The nucleus is a spherical structure found in the centre of an animal cell and a young plant cell, while it occupies a peripheral position in a mature plant cell. It is the most prominent organelle in the cell and constitutes about 10 percent of the cell's volume, and it is separated from the cytoplasm by the nuclear membrane. Generally a cell has only one nucleus (uninucleate); in some cells the nucleus is absent (enucleate), for example red blood cells, while some cells consist of two or more nuclei (multinucleate), for example slime moulds. A nucleus consists of a nuclear membrane, nucleoplasm, nucleolus and chromosomes. The nuclear material is enclosed in a double-layered nuclear membrane whose outer layer is connected to the endoplasmic reticulum, with a fluid-filled space between its two layers, and the membrane has several openings called nuclear pores which provide a passage for exchange of materials like different types of proteins and ribonucleic acids between the nucleus and the cytoplasm. Nucleoplasm, also known as karyoplasm, is the matrix present inside the nucleus; it contains the chromatin network and one or two nucleoli, and during cell division the chromatin network is converted into thick thread-like structures called chromosomes, each composed of deoxyribose nucleic acid (DNA) and a protein called histone. The nucleoli are dark staining bodies, composed of DNA and protein; from the DNA of the nucleoli ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is made, and the nucleoli manufacture and export to the cytoplasm the material responsible for the production of ribosomes, on which proteins are synthesized. Functions: (1) The nucleus is the site of storage of hereditary material in the form of genes, and it also stores different types of proteins and RNA in the nucleolus. (2) Messenger RNA (mRNA) and ribosomes are formed in the nucleus, which are responsible for protein synthesis. (3) It is a site for the exchange of hereditary molecules (DNA and RNA) between the nucleus and the rest of the cell. (4) When the cell divides, the chromatin network breaks into chromosomes, which are then equally transmitted into the offsprings. Diagram (in words): Fig. 8.1 Structure of nucleus shows a large spherical nucleus cut open, with the double outer covering labelled Nuclear Envelope and small openings in it labelled Nuclear Pore. Diagram (in words): Inside the nucleus the thread-like material is labelled Chromatin and the dark round body in the centre is labelled Nucleolus, while outside the nucleus the attached folded membrane is labelled Endoplasmic Reticulum and the small dots on it are labelled Ribosomes.

Q: 2. Describe the importance of hereditary material found in nucleus.

Ans: The hereditary material found in the nucleus is present in the form of chromosomes, genes, DNA and RNA, and the nucleus is the site of its storage. Chromosomes carry genetic information in the form of genes, which are transmitted from one generation to another, and the number of chromosomes is specific in each species, for example it is 46 in man, 26 in frog, 14 in pea and 48 in potato. DNA has a specific sequence of nitrogenous bases, which carries information in the form of genes that can be transferred from generation to generation, and this genetic information is needed to produce a countless number of proteins from various combinations of twenty amino acids, each sequence of bases representing a unique set of genetic instructions. All the characters of living organisms are expressed through genes, which are made up of DNA; genes not only control our body characters but also influence behavioural characteristics like intelligence. During protein synthesis mRNA copies the instructions present in the DNA, each gene coding the instruction for a single protein only, and these instructions are transferred by tRNA and compiled in ribosomes by rRNA into the polypeptide chain of the protein. When the cell divides, the chromatin network breaks into chromosomes which are equally transmitted into the offsprings, so heredity, the transmission of genetic traits to the next generation by reproduction, depends entirely on this hereditary material of the nucleus.

Q: 3. Identify the relationships among nucleic acids (DNA and RNA), genes and chromosomes.

Ans: Nucleic acids are a major class of organic compounds required to maintain life, and nucleic acid molecules are long polymers of smaller building-block units called nucleotides, each nucleotide being composed of a 5-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogen-containing base. Genes are the heredity material and are composed of nucleic acids, and nucleic acids are also the messenger substances that convey information from the genes to the rest of the cell. DNA is a polynucleotide chain, and its most important feature is that it has a specific sequence of nitrogenous bases, which carries information in the form of genes that can be transferred from generation to generation; each gene codes the instruction for a single protein only, and each section of information necessary for the synthesis of a single polypeptide is a gene. A chromosome is composed of DNA and a protein called histone, and chromosomes carry genetic information in the form of genes, so the order of relationship is: the cell contains a nucleus, the nucleus contains chromosomes, and the chromosomes are made of DNA in which the genes lie, as shown in Fig. 8.2 Location of DNA in a cell (Cell, Nucleus, Chromosome, DNA). RNA is the carrier between DNA and protein: DNA itself is not directly involved in protein synthesis and is only the storehouse of genetic information, which is transferred to RNA. There are three types of RNA, messenger RNA (mRNA), transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomal RNA (rRNA), each with its own specific role in protein synthesis: mRNA carries information from the DNA according to which protein is synthesized, tRNA transports amino acids to the site of protein synthesis, and rRNA in the ribosome cooperates with tRNAs to translate mRNAs into peptides, the whole transfer taking place in the two steps of transcription and translation.

Q: 4. Describe the molecular basis of heredity.

Ans: The molecular basis of heredity is the genetic information present in the DNA in the nucleus, so to know the nature of this information we have to see the chemical nature of DNA. DNA is composed of chemical units known as nucleotides, and each nucleotide is composed of smaller parts: a 5-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogen-containing base, both the phosphate group and the nitrogenous base being covalently bonded to the sugar. The nitrogenous bases are of four types, namely adenine, guanine, thymine and cytosine, and the four different types of bases can be arranged in any linear order along a strand of DNA, each sequence of bases representing a unique set of genetic instructions. Watson and Crick proposed the model of the structure of DNA, for which they jointly received the Nobel Prize in 1962 for their 1953 determination of the structure of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): according to this model each DNA molecule is composed of two strands that wind around each other, the sugar-phosphate chain is located on the outer side while the nitrogenous bases project towards the centre. The nitrogenous bases of the two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds; an adenine on one chain always pairs with thymine on the other chain, while guanine always pairs with cytosine, a relationship known as complementarity, the strands being complementary to each other and running in opposite directions. DNA therefore has equal numbers of adenine and thymine (A=T) and equal numbers of guanine and cytosine bases (C=G), so that A+G=T+C, and these relationships help in determining how genetic information is encoded in DNA and passed from one generation to the next, by DNA replication before division and by transfer of the information through RNA to protein synthesis.

Q: 5. Give an overview of the process of DNA replication.

Ans: While describing the structure of DNA, Watson and Crick also proposed the way the DNA molecule can replicate, that is, make an exact copy of itself. During replication, the hydrogen bonds holding the two strands of DNA are broken, causing the gradual separation of the two strands like the two halves of a zipper. Complementary nucleotides present in the cytoplasm then join to form a new strand along the older one, each old strand thus acting as a pattern for a new complementary strand, with adenine pairing with thymine and guanine pairing with cytosine. By completion of the process, two identical molecules of double stranded DNA are formed, so the replication process produces two new DNA molecules from the one original molecule. In this way the same genetic information is available for both daughter cells when the cell divides. Diagram (in words): Fig. 8.9 replication of DNA shows the double helix on the left labelled DNA unwinding and unzipping, free nucleotides in the middle labelled Free nucleotides joining the separated strands, and two new double helices forming on the right labelled New DNA forming.

Q: 6. Describe the process of mitosis in detail.

Ans: Mitosis is the regular process of cell division by which each of the daughter cells receives exactly the same number and the same kind of chromosomes that a parent cell contains. It is a common method, it occurs in the body cells of all animals and plants, and as it occurs in the body (or soma) it is also called somatic cell division. Mitosis is completed in six steps. 1. Interphase: The resting phase between any two mitotic divisions is called interphase; during this phase the nucleus and cytoplasm become active and the nucleus prepares itself for division. 2. Prophase: The centrosome divides into two halves and each half is surrounded by fine fibres called astral rays, which constitute an aster; the two asters move away from each other to the opposite sides of the nucleus, fine fibres appear between them forming a spindle which is broad in the middle at the equator and narrow towards the asters, now known as poles, while the chromatin material of the nucleus is converted into chromosomes, the nucleolus and the nuclear membrane disappear, and the chromosomes attach themselves to the spindle fibres. 3. Metaphase: The centromere of each chromosome divides, and the daughter chromosomes or chromatids so formed are attached to the half spindle fibres and arrange themselves on the equator, forming the equatorial plate. 4. Anaphase: The chromatids separate and the spindle fibres contract, which results in the movement of chromatids towards their respective poles. 5. Telophase: The chromatids reach the poles where they form a chromatin network; in each network the nucleolus reappears and the nuclear membrane is reformed around each chromatin network, so two daughter nuclei are formed, each containing the same number of chromosomes as in the parent cell, and the spindle fibres and astral rays disappear. 6. Cytokinesis: Division of the cytoplasm is called cytokinesis; after the formation of two daughter nuclei a constriction, called the cleavage furrow, appears in the middle of the cytoplasm in the region of the equator, and this furrow deepens and divides the parent cell into two daughter cells, which are exact copies of the parent cell and then pass into interphase and grow to their normal size. Diagram (in words): Fig. 8.10 Different stages of mitosis shows a row of cells labelled in order Interphase (with nucleus and centromeres), Prophase (centromeres, chromosomes appearing), Metaphase (chromosomes on the mitotic spindle, then lined up at the equator), Anaphase (chromatids moving to opposite poles), Telophase (two groups of chromosomes in one cell) and Cytokinesis, ending with the label Cell divides into two daughter cells.

Q: 7. Describe the process of meiosis in detail.

Ans: The term meiosis means reduction: in this type of cell division the number of chromosomes is reduced to half. This process occurs in the reproductive organs (testes or ovaries); in animals meiosis produces gametes while in plants it produces spores, and during meiosis four daughter cells are formed from one parent cell. Meiosis is completed in two steps, Meiosis I and Meiosis II. I. Meiosis I or Reduction Division: (A) Prophase I: Coiling and condensation of chromosomes take place, the homologous chromosomes form pairs, a process called synapsis, and later crossing over between the homologous chromosomes takes place, during which the chromatids exchange their parts; the nuclear membrane disappears, spindle fibres are formed and the chromosomes are attached to the spindle fibres. (B) Metaphase I: The chromosomes arrange themselves on the equator, attached to the spindle fibres by the centromere. (C) Anaphase I: Contraction of spindle fibres occurs and the chromosomes start movement from the equator towards the poles; reduction of chromosomes occurs at this stage, as one from each pair of chromosomes moves to each pole. (D) Telophase I: The chromosomes reach the poles and form a chromatin network, the nuclear membrane appears around the network and a new nucleolus appears, so two daughter nuclei are formed; then a groove is formed in the cell membrane, which becomes deeper and deeper and divides the cell into two daughter cells, the spindle fibres and astral rays disappear and the centriole persists in each daughter cell. II. Meiosis II: Meiosis II is just like mitosis and is completed through the steps 1. Prophase II, 2. Metaphase II, 3. Anaphase II and 4. Telophase II. After the first cell division each resulting cell contains a pair of sister chromatids, one maternal chromatid and the other paternal; unlike mitosis, meiosis does not end after one division but continues with a second cell division, in which the sister chromatids are separated, producing four haploid cells. Significance: gametes are formed, which are the sexual units of reproduction; meiosis maintains a constant number of chromosomes in the organism by the union of haploid cells during sexual reproduction; and meiosis causes exchange of genes, so genetic variation occurs among the species. Diagram (in words): Fig. 8.11 Different stages of meiosis shows at the top a Cell nucleus labelled Chromosomes from parents, then Chromosomes replicate, then Matching chromosomes pair up, then Chromosomes swap sections of DNA, which creates a mix of new genetic material in the offspring's cells; the chromosome pairs divide into two daughter nuclei, the daughter nuclei divide again, and four final cells are formed with single chromosomes and a new mix of genetic material.

Q: 8. Explain thalassemia and Down's syndrome as common genetic disorders.

Ans: Genetic diseases are those disorders which are transmitted from parents to offsprings, and thalassemia and Down's syndrome are two common examples. Thalassemia: Thalassemia is a blood disorder which is hereditary in nature. In this disorder the body makes an abnormal form of haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen, because there is a defect in a gene that controls the production of haemoglobin; thalassemia is caused by mutations in the DNA of cells that make haemoglobin. The disorder results in excessive destruction of red blood cells, which leads to anaemia, the condition in which the body does not have enough healthy red blood cells to provide oxygen to body tissues, and Fig. 8.12 compares normal red blood cells with the malformed red blood cells of thalassemia, along with white blood cells and platelets. Untreated thalassemia leads to heart failure and liver problems and makes a person vulnerable to infections; frequent blood transfusions can help control some symptoms, but they may result in accumulation of iron, which can damage the heart, liver and endocrine system. Down's syndrome: In a human being there are 23 pairs of chromosomes, each chromosomal pair numbered from 1 to 23. Down's syndrome is a chromosomal disorder concerned with chromosome number 21, where instead of a pair there are three chromosomes, so an extra chromosome is present and the total becomes 47 instead of 46. This disorder is commonly known in the book as Mongolism, as the facial features of these people were described as looking like Mongols. Down's syndrome includes characteristic facial features, short stature, heart defects, susceptibility to respiratory infection and mental retardation (the book's term for intellectual disability).

Q: 9. Analyze the role of genetic engineering and biotechnology in the fields of agriculture and food processing.

Ans: Genetic engineering is a technique used for the transfer of genes from one organism to another, allowing genetic information to be transferred between organisms belonging to the same or different species, while biotechnology is the commercial application of living organisms or their products which involves the deliberate manipulation of their DNA molecules. In agriculture: Agricultural biotechnology is the area of biotechnology involving applications to agriculture. It has been practised for a long time, as people have sought to improve agriculturally important plants by selective breeding; an example of traditional agricultural biotechnology is the development of disease-resistant wheat varieties by cross-breeding different wheat types. Today the technology has reached a stage where scientists can take one or more specific genes from nearly any organism, including plants, animals, bacteria or viruses, and introduce those genes into plants to get the required characteristics in those plants. In this way the traditional method of plant breeding is being replaced by the creation of transgenic plants, which have genes for resisting infections and attacking insects, so biotech crops are more profitable and productive. In food processing: Biotechnology is defined in the introduction as the use of living microorganisms or biological processes for industrial, agricultural or medicinal processes for the welfare of man, and man has used the ability of microorganisms to carry out fermentation for hundreds of years to produce foods such as yogurt, cheese and bread, all made by the fermentation process brought about by yeast, bacteria or fungi; citric acid is also produced commercially by the action of bacteria or fungi. In food processing techniques biotechnology helps to convert relatively bulky, perishable and typically inedible raw materials into more useful and edible foods and drinks, and food is also processed in order to improve its quality and safety. Thus in both fields the same principle works: useful genes and useful microorganisms are used deliberately to obtain better crops and better, safer food for man.

Key Points

  • Underground water is found in the cracks and crevices in soil, sand and rocks and slowly moves through aquifers
  • Freshwater is water which contains less than 1000 milligrams per liter of salts
  • Only about 3 percent of the global water supply is freshwater
  • Potable water is water which is considered safe for consumption both for humans and animals
  • Major pressures on water resources include urbanization, population growth, increased living standards, growing competition for water, and pollution
  • Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the roots of crops and saves precious water
  • Climate change has resulted in heavy rains causing floods and in extreme hot and dry conditions
  • The shrinking and melting of glaciers is clear evidence of climate change noticed in many parts of the world

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Write short answers of the following questions

Q: 1. Enlist various forms of water available on the Earth.

Ans: The book lists the major forms of water on Earth as: (1) oceans and seas, which are the largest bodies of water and hold saline water; (2) lakes, small standing bodies of fresh water; (3) rivers, flowing bodies of water that carry water from the land to the sea; (4) springs, water that comes out at points on the land surface; (5) glaciers, snow compressed over many years into large ice masses; and (6) underground water, found in cracks and crevices in soil, sand and rocks and held in aquifers. Water is also present in the air as water vapours, in icecaps, and in the ground as soil moisture.

Q: 2. What do you mean by underground water?

Ans: Underground water (ground water) is the water found in the cracks and crevices in soil, sand and rocks. It slowly moves through aquifers and is extracted through water wells and tube wells. It plays an important role in the irrigation of agricultural lands and is also used for domestic consumption and industrial use. Its availability depends on the water table, which is the upper level of the underground surface where soil or rocks are permanently saturated with water. Diagram (in words): In the water cycle (Fig. 9.17), rain water enters the ground by Infiltration and collects below the surface as Ground water storage, from where it can rise again through a Spring.

Q: 3. What do you mean by freshwater. Why it is important to us?

Ans: Freshwater is water which contains less than 1000 milligrams per liter of salts. Only about 3 percent of the global water supply is freshwater, the remaining about 97 percent being saline water in the oceans. Freshwater is important to us because it is the water that can be used for drinking purposes and domestic consumption. It is also the water used for irrigation, industry and other human activities, and only a very small part of the world's total water is suitable for human use.

Q: 4. What do you mean by potable water?

Ans: Potable water, or drinking water, is the water which is considered safe for consumption both for humans and animals. Natural freshwater sources like springs, lakes and rivers, if not contaminated by human activities, provide safe water for human consumption. Contaminated drinking water, together with poor sanitation, causes diseases like diarrhea and dysentery, so water is treated before it is pumped for distribution. Diagram (in words): In a water treatment plant (Fig. 9.20), water from wells, lakes or rivers passes in order through Coagulation, where special compounds remove the dirt particles from the water; Sedimentation, where the dirt settles to the bottom and the water becomes cleaner; Filtration, where water passes through filters to purify it further; and Disinfection, which kills the germs, after which the treated water goes from the water tower to homes.

Q: 5. Enlist major pressures on water resources.

Ans: According to the book, pressures on water resources are increasing mainly as a result of human activity. The major pressures are: urbanization, population growth, increased living standards, growing competition for water, and pollution. Water resources are also threatened by unwise and unplanned human activities, worldwide competition for controlling water resources, and the adverse effects of climate change.

Q: 6. Give three main measures for sustainable development of water resources of Pakistan.

Ans: Three main measures given in the book are: (1) Improving planning, management and community participation in the utilization of local water systems, with a regular programme for cleaning canals and waterways. (2) Proper lining of the canal system, because a huge amount of water is lost due to seepage from canals, and using efficient irrigation techniques such as drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to the roots of crops and saves precious water. (3) Storage of flood water during the monsoon season by construction of small dams, especially in the barrani areas, and construction of mega dams to store a huge amount of flood water and provide water for irrigation.

Q: 7. Give a brief account of climate change on water resources.

Ans: Globally, climate change has resulted in heavy rains causing floods and in extreme hot and dry conditions. Global warming and the rise in temperature have resulted in higher rates of evaporation and warm air holding intense rainstorms, bringing large amounts of water which flow down into the rivers and streams, while the soil remains dry and the risk of drought increases. One clear evidence of climate change is the shrinking and melting of glaciers, which has already been noticed in many parts of the world. Diagram (in words): The water cycle (Fig. 9.17) shows how water circulates between the atmosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere: Evaporation lifts water from Water storage in oceans, and Evapotranspiration lifts it from land and plants; the vapour undergoes Condensation in clouds and falls back as precipitation; on the mountains it is held as Water storage in ice and snow, and Snow melt runoff to streams joins Stream flow; on the land it moves as Surface runoff, enters the soil by Infiltration to Ground water storage, and may come out again at a Spring, before finally returning to the sea.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • About 71 percent of the Earth surface is covered by water
  • About 69 percent of the total freshwater available on Earth is held by the glaciers and permanent ice sheets of the arctic region
  • Agriculture accounts for about 70 percent of the total usable water globally
  • In Pakistan agriculture uses 93 percent of the water, industry uses 5 percent and public use is 2 percent
  • The canal infrastructure in Pakistan loses about two-third of the water due to poor transmission and seepage
  • Reclamation of water means to reclaim usable water from waste waters and use it for irrigation and other purposes
  • In secondary treatment of waste water, bacteria are added so that they ingest organic wastes
  • Approximately 2 billion people are currently living in areas faced with water stress and scarcity
  • Tree roots hold precious soil and allow more water to be absorbed by the soil and moved to underground water reservoirs

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Write in detail answers of the following questions

Q: 1. Identify the amount of fresh water available on Earth with an emphasis on Pakistan.

Ans: About 71 percent of the Earth's surface is covered by water, and about 96.5 percent of all Earth's water is present in the oceans, which is saline in nature. Freshwater, defined as water containing less than 1000 milligrams per liter of salts, is only about 3 percent of the global water supply (2.5 percent in Fig. 9.1), and it is this small part that can be used for drinking purposes and domestic consumption. Of the total freshwater available on Earth, about 69 percent is held by the glaciers and permanent ice sheets of the arctic region, underground water accounts for approximately 30 percent of the total freshwater supply, and the rest is present in lakes, streams and springs, with minute amounts stored in the soil, the atmosphere and in biological organisms. Emphasis on Pakistan: Pakistan has plenty of fresh water resources in the form of surface water, rainfall and groundwater. Rivers and fresh water lakes constitute the surface water resources, and the river system is mainly based on the Indus River and its tributaries: the five major eastern tributaries Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, the minor tributaries Soan, Harow and Siran, and the River Kabul, the biggest western tributary. Monsoon rains constitute about 70 percent of the annual rainfall, occurring from June to September, but much of this flood water drains into the Arabian Sea without giving any benefit. Pakistan also has a rich groundwater resource: the Indus Plain extends from the Himalayan foothills to the Arabian Sea for about 1,600 km, and its rich alluvial deposits hold extensive unconfined aquifers used for domestic consumption and irrigation.

Q: 2. The level of agricultural production is directly related to the availability and effective use of water as a major input. Justify the statement.

Ans: The statement is justified by the place of water in agriculture as described in the chapter. The agricultural sector is the largest consumer of water: globally, agriculture accounts for about 70 percent of the total usable water, and for as much as 95 percent of water use in predominantly agriculture-based countries. In Pakistan, Fig. 9.6 shows agriculture using 93 percent of the water, against 5 percent for industry and 2 percent for public use. Pakistan has a total area of 79.6 million hectares, about 27 percent of which is under cultivation, and almost 80 percent of the current cropped area is irrigated with the help of canals; Pakistan has one of the largest canal systems in the world. Rivers are the main source of water for irrigation, and melting water from mountainous glaciers adds to their flow. Because agricultural productivity determines the status of global food security, the availability or scarcity of water directly impacts food security: where water is available and used effectively, crops grow and production rises, while misuse, wastage and scarcity reduce the yield. With population growth, food demand at the global level is expected to almost double in the coming few decades, and food production will demand still more water, which shows that the level of agricultural production rises or falls with the availability and effective use of water.

Q: 3. Describe the existing ways of utilization of water resources in Pakistan.

Ans: In Pakistan, water resources are used in three broad categories. Firstly, domestic use: water is used in domestic activities, which include drinking, cooking, bathing, washing etc. (public/domestic use is 2 percent in Fig. 9.6). Secondly, industrial and manufacturing use (5 percent): industries related to metals production, wood and paper products, chemicals etc. consume large quantities of water, and in industries water is used in processing, washing, diluting, cooling, or transporting a product. Thirdly, agricultural use, which is the largest consumer of water (93 percent): Pakistan has a total area of 79.6 million hectares, about 27 percent of the area is currently under cultivation, and almost 80 percent of the current cropped area is irrigated with the help of canals, so Pakistan has one of the largest canal systems in the world and one of the highest proportions of irrigated cropped area. Apart from these, Pakistan has built several water reservoirs and dams; these reservoirs are not only producing energy (hydropower) but also have a key role in managing the irrigation system of Pakistan. The water itself comes from rivers flowing down from the Himalayan and Karakoram ranges, with melting water from mountainous glaciers adding to the flow of the rivers, and from groundwater extracted through wells and tube wells.

Q: 4. Explain the issues and problems Pakistan is facing in utilizing the water resources effectively for its people.

Ans: Pakistan's water resources heavily depend on winter snowfall and monsoon rains, and this weather phenomenon is limited to certain areas, so the rest of the country receives very little rainfall and people living in such areas have little or no access to surface water. At present the resources are declining and being degraded by several problems: over-exploitation of groundwater, misuse and wastage of surface water, and vulnerability of water resources to different kinds of pollution. To increase agricultural yield and feed the ever increasing population, groundwater is pumped extensively or too much water is diverted from the rivers for irrigation, and these practices result in the formation of salinity and degradation of fertile land, which can lead to food scarcity in the long run. Although Pakistan has one of the largest irrigation systems in the world, the canal infrastructure loses about two-third of the water due to poor transmission and seepage, which in turn causes waterlogging and salinity. Lack of access to clean drinking water is a leading cause of diseases such as diarrhea, typhoid, cholera, malaria and dysentery. Pakistan is also among the countries that can be severely affected by climatic changes, which would make its water resources vulnerable. The book concludes that a big investment in the repair of existing dams and large scale construction of new water reservoirs is the first step in conserving the water resources of Pakistan, and that a proper water management strategy should be devised to tackle these challenges.

Q: 5. Explain the methods of reclamation of water.

Ans: Reclamation of water means to reclaim usable water from waste waters and to use this water for irrigation and for other purposes; reclamation strategies are initiated at places where abundant waste water is generated. The method described in the book has the following stages. (1) Primary treatment: sewage is sent for primary treatment, in which water is separated from large particles, after which it enters sedimentation tanks; solid particles settle at the bottom and waste water is separated. (2) Secondary treatment: after primary treatment, waste water is sent for secondary treatment, where bacteria are added to the waste water so that they ingest organic wastes. (3) Tertiary treatment: the waste water is filtered and is disinfected with chlorine, and any leftover salt is removed. (4) Advanced treatment for drinking: for recycled water to become drinkable, tertiary-treated water undergoes advanced water treatment technology; the water is then disinfected by ultra violet light (UV) or hydrogen peroxide, and finally it is added to groundwater or surface water reservoirs, where it stays for several months to be further purified by natural processes. In this way waste water, instead of being thrown away, is reclaimed and used again, just as water in nature is continuously recycled through the hydrological cycle.

Q: 6. Write an essay on conservation of water.

Ans: Water is a key resource, and although it is a renewable resource that continuously circulates through the hydrological cycle from the sea to air and land and back to the sea, the sources of usable and drinkable water are limited. The best strategy in natural resource management is therefore to use the resource wisely and make strategies for its conservation, so that the coming generations have an equal chance to take benefits from the resource too; this needs serious efforts both at the individual and at the government level. At the individual and home level, precious water can be saved by simple measures: closing the tap while cleaning your teeth; making sure that taps and showers are closed; and doing necessary repairs for leaking and damaged water pipes. Rain water can be collected and used for gardening and washing, as shown in the rain harvesting system (Fig. 9.10), where collection pipes transfer rainwater to a tank, the collected rainwater is filtered before use, and the remaining water can be sent to a harvesting well deep enough to connect to the ground water table. In agriculture, water can be saved by using efficient irrigation techniques, for example drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to the roots of crops, and overhead irrigation. To recharge underground water, recharge pits can be dug for storing rainwater and stopping runoff water, giving the land ample time to recharge the ground water supply. Increasing the vegetation cover and planting more trees can also stop runoff water. At the larger level, storing surplus water in large water reservoirs during the rainfall season makes water available for irrigation in dry spells and controls flooding during the rainy season; in Pakistan, investment in the repair of existing dams and construction of new reservoirs is a first step. Conserving water in these ways protects the resource for future generations and prevents water crisis, famine and ecological disaster.

Q: 7. Explain how water resources are being threatened by urbanization and deforestation.

Ans: Urbanization: The process of urbanization has resulted in the haphazard development of residential and industrial areas in large cities, and these areas are the main source of point-source pollution. Development of roads, infrastructure and other human activities puts stress on precious natural resources, including the water resource of that area. Domestic wastewater combined with untreated industrial waste poses a serious threat, and the ill managed sanitation system and sewage treatment is a threat to water bodies; nearby water bodies are often used for releasing untreated water from urban areas and industries, so rivers in developing countries are more like open sewers than rivers. Garbage collection and disposal facilities are lacking in most cases, so polythene bags and other solid wastes are seen in streams and rivers, and in these conditions the fish population has almost become non-existent. Coastal urban centres dump untreated sewage in the sea, which contaminates beaches, affects the marine habitat and poses a serious threat to people who visit the beaches. Deforestation: Trees are cut to clear land for agriculture, for the establishment of industrial zones, infrastructure and residential areas. Once the land is exposed, it is open to all types of environmental hazards; exposed land is vulnerable to erosion, which results in the loss of soil nutrients and consequently the fertility of the land is lost. Forests also play an important role in the regulation and maintenance of the water cycle: the roots of the trees not only hold precious soil but allow more water to be absorbed by the soil and move this water to the underground water reservoirs, so cutting forests disturbs the water cycle and reduces groundwater recharge. Together, urbanization and deforestation pollute, waste and deplete the water resources of an area.

Q: 8. Describe the implications of growing demand of water in the world.

Ans: Water used for human consumption is limited in quantity: only 1 percent of the total amount of water present on planet Earth can be utilized (the exercise puts the suitable share at less than 1 percent). Because of this, competition for water resources is growing, and its effects are evident from the rising tensions between different countries and nations in different parts of the world; water shortage has even become the cause of conflicts, as in Darfur (Sudan). Water is vital for survival, and its scarcity affects every sphere of life, i.e. social, political and economic, and it even threatens the health of the ecological system; according to one estimate, approximately 2 billion people are currently living in areas faced with water stress and scarcity. The sharp rise in human population over the last many decades is a major contributor to water scarcity, because population growth limits the amount of water available per person and means mounting demand and competition for water in agriculture, domestic, industrial and municipal uses. Population growth demands more food, and more water is needed to produce that food, since in the agriculture sector water is mainly used for irrigation; food production is expected to demand more water and put extra pressure on already depleting resources. Growing industrialization increases the use of water for cooling, processing and disposal of waste products, and growing urbanization, especially in developing countries, puts pressure on water resources while increased pollution depletes usable water, making people vulnerable to water shortages and increasing per capita consumption. Poor water quality and unsustainable use can limit the economic development of a country, harm health and affect livelihoods: water related diseases are a major health problem in many parts of the world and children are more vulnerable to water borne diseases, while the lack of clean drinking water forces women and young girls to fetch water from far flung areas, affecting their health and diminishing their educational opportunities. The overall implication is that, although the water cycle renews itself at the global level, usable water is depleting with every passing moment, so sustainable development of water resources is the right step for saving this precious resource for the generations to come.

Key Points

  • The lithosphere is not a layer of the Earth's atmosphere, unlike the troposphere, stratosphere and thermosphere
  • Sulphur dioxide is the gas named in the exercise as a cause of acid rain
  • Ultraviolet radiations from the sun that reach the Earth can cause skin cancer
  • Chlorofluorocarbons are not a pollutant produced by vehicle exhaust, unlike carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and nitrogen oxide
  • Oxygen is not a greenhouse gas, while carbon dioxide, chlorofluorocarbons and methane are greenhouse gases
  • The ozone layer is present in the stratosphere and ozone absorbs the ultraviolet radiations there
  • Lead is the most hazardous metal pollutant in automobile exhaust
  • Water pollution is primarily caused by human activities
