mcqs.q: All of the following are layers of earth's atmosphere EXCEPT:
mcqs.why: The lithosphere is the solid rocky shell of the Earth, not a layer of the atmosphere, while the troposphere, stratosphere and thermosphere are all layers of the atmosphere named in this unit.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following causes acid rain?
mcqs.why: Sulphur dioxide released by burning fossil fuels dissolves in rainwater to form sulphuric acid, and rain containing this acid falls as acid rain.

mcqs.why: Ultraviolet radiations that reach the Earth's surface damage the skin and cause skin cancer, which is also listed in the unit as a major effect of ozone depletion.

mcqs.why: Vehicle exhaust produces carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and nitrogen oxide, but chlorofluorocarbons come from sources such as refrigerators, air conditioners and insulation foam, not from vehicle exhaust.

mcqs.q: Ozone layer is present in:
mcqs.why: The ozone layer is a layer of ozone encircling the planet within the stratosphere, about 10 to 45 kilometres above the Earth's surface.

mcqs.q: The ultraviolet radiations in stratosphere are absorbed by:
mcqs.why: Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs 97 to 99 percent of the harmful ultraviolet radiations emitted by the sun, shielding the Earth from them.

mcqs.q: Most hazardous metal pollutant in the automobile exhaust is:
mcqs.why: Lead released in automobile exhaust is the most hazardous metal pollutant named in the exercise, which is why the unit recommends using lead free petrol in vehicles.

mcqs.q: Which of the following gases contribute to the greenhouse effect on earth?
mcqs.why: Carbon dioxide, methane and chlorofluorocarbons are all greenhouse gases that trap heat in the atmosphere, so the book's keyed answer naming all three of them is given here as one combined option.

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT an expected effect of climate change?

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a non-point source of water pollution?

  • Desertification is land degradation caused by climatic variations and human activities in which productive land changes into desert
  • The greenhouse effect can be controlled by reducing fossil fuel and wood burning, using electricity and solar energy, increasing forest area and eliminating chlorofluorocarbons completely
  • Natural disasters are tremendous changes inside or on the surface of the Earth that are exhibited as floods, droughts, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, cyclones, avalanches and forest fires
  • The layers of the atmosphere named in this unit are the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere and thermosphere
  • Climate is the set of average weather conditions of an area sustained over many years and it depends on sunlight, altitude, distance from the sea, vegetation cover, wind, rainfall pattern and topography
  • Human activities degrade agricultural land through erosion, water logging and salinity linked to increased use of nitrogenous fertilizers and irrigation
  • Air pollution from human activities produces photochemical smog, acid deposition, the greenhouse effect and destruction of the ozone shield

Exercise B: Write short answers of the following questions

Q: 1. Give a brief overview of the nature of ozone layer found in the atmosphere.

Ans: About 10-45 kilometres above the Earth's surface there is a layer of ozone encircling our planet, present in the stratosphere part of the atmosphere. It shields the Earth from most of the ultraviolet radiations coming from the sun. The ozone layer is capable of absorbing 97-99% of the harmful ultraviolet radiations emitted by the sun.

Q: 2. Define the term desertification.

Ans: Desertification is defined as land degradation resulting from various factors including climatic variations and human activities. In this process a productive land, either through climatic variations or through unwise utilization by humans, gets degraded and changes into desert.

Q: 3. List some measures to control the green house effect.

Ans: The greenhouse effect and global warming can be controlled by preventing the release of larger quantities of greenhouse gases, by reducing the tremendous use of fossil fuel and wood for burning. The use of fossil fuels can also be reduced by using alternate means like electricity and solar energy. An increase in the forest area is also a good remedy to reduce carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, and the manufacture and use of CFCs should be eliminated completely.

Q: 4. What are natural disasters and in which forms these are exhibited?

Ans: Natural disasters are the tremendous changes which occur deep inside the Earth or on its surface and which are so great that they may cause damage to the shape of the land or to the lives of people and other living things. They are exhibited in the form of floods, droughts, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, cyclones or hurricanes, avalanches and forest fires etc.

Q: 5. Enlist the names of different layers of atmosphere.

Ans: The layers of the atmosphere named in this unit are: (i) Troposphere — the lowest layer, shown below the ozone layer in Fig. 10.2; (ii) Stratosphere — the layer in which the ozone layer is present; (iii) Mesosphere; and (iv) Thermosphere.

Q: 6. Define climate.

Ans: Different regions of the world are characterized by different sets of climatic conditions which sustain themselves over a period of many years, and on the basis of these average weather conditions we say that a certain area has a particular type of climate. The climate of an area depends upon the amount of sunlight it receives and on geographic factors like altitude, distance from the sea, vegetation cover, wind, rainfall pattern and topography of the area.

Q: 7. Write five major effects on environment by human activities.

Ans: Five major effects of human activities on the environment given in this unit are: (1) environmental degradation and climatic change with global impacts; (2) land degradation — land erosion, water logging and salinity of precious agricultural lands due to increased use of nitrogenous fertilizers and irrigation; (3) damage to natural ecological systems and loss of biodiversity when forests and natural grasslands are transformed into farmlands; (4) air pollution producing photochemical smog, acid deposition, greenhouse effect and ozone shield destruction; and (5) pollution of air, water, soil and food by solid and hazardous wastes in liquid, solid or gaseous forms.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Chlorofluorocarbons such as Freon release active chlorine in the stratosphere and a single chlorine atom destroys about 100,000 molecules of ozone
  • Ozone depletion lets higher levels of ultraviolet radiation reach the Earth, causing skin cancer, eye cataracts, weak immunity and damage to crops
  • Global warming is the rise in Earth's temperature caused mainly by greenhouse gases because carbon dioxide lets solar radiation in but traps heat that would otherwise escape to space
  • Acid rain forms when sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides dissolve in rainwater to make sulphuric acid and nitric acid
  • Acid rain damages plant leaves, poisons fish through aluminium salts washed into rivers and lakes, and corrodes limestone and marble buildings through stone cancer
  • Signs of climate change include shortening winters, shrinking ice cover, dying coral reefs, more mosquito-borne diseases, rising sea levels and more common extreme weather
  • El Niño is the warm phase and La Niña is the cold phase of a Pacific ocean and atmosphere cycle that lasts 9 to 12 months and repeats every three to five years
  • International environmental law began as a separate field at the Stockholm Conference on Environment in 1972 and its scope covers pollution control and remediation plus conservation of natural resources

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Write in detail answers of the following questions

Q: 1. What are the main causes of ozone depletion? List some of the major effects of ozone depletion on the living organisms.

Ans: Causes: The depletion of ozone became known in 1985 with the discovery of a big hole in the ozone layer over the Antarctica continent. The loss of ozone is caused by commercially important compounds called chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), of which the most important is Freon. When a CFC drifts up into the stratosphere it releases active chlorine, which reacts with the ozone molecules of the ozone shield, and a single atom of chlorine destroys about 100,000 molecules of ozone. CFCs are used as coolants in air conditioners and refrigerators, as foam for insulation and packaging, and as medical sterilizers. Effects: With the depletion of the ozone layer, higher levels of ultraviolet radiations reach the surface of the Earth. This causes skin cancer, eye cataracts, weak immunity and damage to crops. Diagram (in words): Fig. 10.2 'Ozone layer depletion' shows the sun at the top right sending Solar radiation down towards the Earth. Below the sun is the band labelled Stratosphere, and within it the dark band labelled Ozone layer. Beneath the ozone layer lies the Troposphere, above the Earth's surface with houses and factories. Wavy arrows labelled CFC's etc. rise from the factories and houses on the surface up through the Troposphere and break through the ozone layer at the points labelled Ozone depletion. Through these depleted parts, wavy arrows labelled Harmful UV rays pass down from above and reach the Earth's surface.

Q: 2. Describe global warming and its consequences.

Ans: Global warming is an increase in the Earth's temperature due to the effect of the greenhouse gases, mainly carbon dioxide, methane and some other gases. The greenhouse effect in the atmosphere causes global warming: carbon dioxide in the atmosphere allows solar radiations to pass through, but does not permit heat to radiate back into space; instead, the heat is reflected back to the Earth's surface, which heats up the atmosphere of the Earth. During the past several decades greenhouse gases have accumulated to such an extent that the Earth's temperature has increased by 0.8°C as a result of this phenomenon. Consequences: Global warming produces harmful effects such as melting of polar ice resulting in rising of sea level, changes in the rainfall pattern, migration and extinction of some animals, and increasing the frequency and duration of droughts and hurricanes. The Key Points also list flooding, climate change and diseases among its results.

Q: 3. How acid rain is caused? What impacts this rain can have on the life of living organisms of a particular region?

Ans: Cause: Acid rain is rain that has a larger amount of acid in it than normal rain, and it is one of the most dangerous forms of air pollution. It is caused by smoke and gases given off by factories and automobiles that run on fossil fuels, especially coal. When these fuels are burnt to produce energy, the sulphur present in the fuel combines with oxygen and becomes sulphur dioxide; at the same time some of the nitrogen in the air converts into nitrogen oxide. Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere dissolve in rainwater to form sulphuric acid and nitric acid respectively, and rain containing these acids is known as acid rain. Impacts: When acid rain falls on plants, it damages their leaves and retards their growth. Falling on the earth, acid rain dissolves aluminium salts in the soil and washes them into rivers and lakes, and these salts in higher concentration are poisonous to fish and other marine life. It also damages buildings and historic monuments, especially those made of limestone and marble: when it falls on buildings it slowly dissolves the limestones and mortar, and the acids react with calcium compounds in the stones to create gypsum, which then flakes off — the phenomenon termed stone cancer.

Q: 4. What do you mean by Climate change? Describe some of its effects.

Ans: Meaning: Climate is the set of average weather conditions of an area sustained over many years. Climatic change on a global scale is either due to the amount of heat that is let into the system, or the amount of heat that is let out of the system. In the recent past there has been a constant accumulation of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, which has resulted in global warming: global temperatures in the past one hundred years have been increasing more rapidly than the historic record shows, and this increase has been attributed to increasing amounts of greenhouse gases trapping heat. Effects: In addition to a rise in average global temperature, the changes that indicate that climate is indeed changing include shortening of winter, fast shrinking of the Earth's ice cover (for example, the melting of Greenland's ice sheet), killing of coral reefs due to warming sea water, increase in mosquito-borne diseases, rising sea levels, increased precipitation (rainfall etc.) in most areas, and extreme weather becoming more common.

Q: 5. Describe natural disasters caused by El-Nino and La-Nina.

Ans: El Niño and La Niña are the two phases of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle, the phenomenon in which a change in temperature between the ocean and atmosphere takes place in the east-central Equatorial Pacific region; La Niña is the cold phase and El Niño is the warm phase, and the cycle lasts for 9 to 12 months and is repeated after every three to five years. El Niño results in an increase in the average ocean surface water temperature in the region and causes climatic change around the world: it causes torrential rains across the west coast of North America and South America, and the warm water reduces the fish population. Strong rains and damages caused by flooding were noticed from 1965-1966, 1982-1983 and 1997-1998, and California to Mexico to Chile were the worst affected regions. La Niña is responsible for the opposite effects on climate as El Niño; for example, a major La Niña event in 1988 caused significant drought across North America.

Q: 6. Identify the legislation or laws on environmental problems.

Ans: International environmental law was introduced as a separate area of public international law in the Stockholm Conference on Environment in 1972, and since then the need for legislation in the field of environment has increased gradually. At the international level, cooperation has been fostered by treaties, resolutions and agreements finalized by intergovernmental organizations, while at home countries are having national laws and regulations to protect the environment. The scope of environmental laws can be summarized into two categories: firstly, pollution control and remediation, and secondly, conservation of natural resources. The important international laws pertaining to environmental issues listed in the book are: (1) Convention on Biological Diversity; (2) Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species; (3) Framework Convention on Climate Change; (4) Law of the Sea (LOS); and (5) Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants. The issues in focus include destruction of tropical rain forests, ozone layer depletion and global warming, international trade in endangered species, protection of wetlands, transboundary nuclear air pollution, dumping of hazardous wastes, groundwater depletion and oil spills.

Q: 7. Describe the control strategies that can be used for treating air pollutants.

Ans: The book gives the following methods to reduce air pollution, which are the control strategies for air pollutants such as nitrogen oxide, hydrocarbons, sulphur dioxide, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, methane, chlorofluorocarbons and halogens (Table 10.1): (i) We can cut down the burning of fossil fuel by using alternative means like biomass energy, solar energy etc.; (ii) In the field of agriculture, the use of pesticides can be reduced by using new varieties of plants which are pest resistant; (iii) Lead free petrol can be used in vehicles; (iv) Deforestation should be checked and more plants should be grown; (v) Emission from industries should be controlled and treated before releasing them into the atmosphere, and by following strict laws; (vi) Use of refrigerators, air conditioners, air fresheners etc. may be reduced to reduce the amount of CFCs emissions.

Q: 8. Describe the harmful effects of the excessive use of Television on individual's health.

Ans: Television in moderation is a good activity, as it is an excellent educator and entertainer, but watching too much television is harmful. Children are glued to television and spend maximum time watching their favourite programs; recent research suggests that children who spend more than 4 hours continuously per day watching TV are more likely to be overweight, and in much older people it can lead to obesity and heart diseases. When you watch television your thinking mechanism stops, and you can be easily misinformed and manipulated into forming an opinion that is not your own but is based on the analysis of those who produced the programs. Watching too much television often leads to behavioural changes: young children who watch aggressive cartoons and movies become violent and develop a destructive nature. Social development is also affected because of the time spent watching television instead of playing sports in the playground, and television even influences spending habits, as advertisements project wrong information in a glamorous way. The book therefore advises watching television in moderation and using one's thinking and analytical abilities before making opinions and choices.

Key Points

  • Both MRI and CT scan produce cross-sectional internal images of the body with the help of a computer.
  • A CT scan uses X-rays, while an MRI scan uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves.
  • Lasers are used in telecommunications, microsurgery, bar-code scanners, printers and holography.
  • Optical fibers carry digital signals as pulses of light by total internal reflection.
  • About one-quarter pound of optical fiber can transmit the same amount of information as 33 tons of copper.
  • Artificial satellites relay speech, conversation and pictures over electromagnetic waves to far-off places on Earth.
  • A mobile phone gives a user wireless connectivity to a nearby transmitter while moving between areas of coverage.
  • EEG records the electrical activity of the brain, while ECG records the bio-electric currents generated by the heart.
  • MRI is safer than CT scan because it does not use X-rays, which are ionizing radiations that can be harmful.
  • A computer processes the data entered into it and gives out the result rapidly, with high speed, accuracy and large memory.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Write short answers of the following questions

Q: 1. What are the similarities and differences between MRI and CT scan.

Ans: Similarity: both MRI and CT scan produce cross-sectional internal images of the body with the help of a computer, and both help doctors diagnose abnormal conditions developing inside the body. Difference: a CT scan is a special type of X-ray test that uses X-rays to make its images, while an MRI scan does not use X-rays at all — it uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to produce very clear and detailed two- and three-dimensional images.

Q: 2. How laser is used in different scientific processes.

Ans: Lasers have opened a new field of scientific research and are widely used in many ways. They are used in telecommunications in space and in open-air communications, for microsurgery of different body organs, in bar-code scanners and in printers for superior quality computer print outs, and to generate three-dimensional images of objects in the process called holography. Lasers are also used in research instruments such as CD and DVD players.

Q: 3. Why optical fiber is better than copper cable for telecommunication?

Ans: Optical fibers carry digital signals as pulses of light by total internal reflection, so they give high data transmission rates and a much higher carrying capacity than copper cable — about 1/4 pound of optical fiber can transmit the same amount of information as 33 tons of copper. They are thinner, lighter and less expensive, data travels in them with maximum protection and very less losses, and because they carry beams of light they are free of electrical noise and interference.

Q: 4. What is the importance of artificial satellite in telecommunication?

Ans: Artificial satellites move around the Earth and are used to relay messages, e.g. speech, conversation and pictures, transmitted over electromagnetic waves from one place to far off places on the Earth's surface. In this way they make instant long-distance communication possible and enable us to view live events and matches on television in distant parts of the world.

Q: 5. How has mobile phone changed the life style of the people of Pakistan?

Ans: The mobile or cell phone has revolutionized communication technology, and in Pakistan mobile phone users are increasing with every passing day. A mobile phone gives a user wireless connectivity to a nearby transmitter, so people can speak to each other from anywhere while moving from one area of coverage to another. It has made instant contact possible at all times, which has changed the daily life style, work and social contacts of the people of Pakistan.

Q: 6. Differentiate between EEG and ECG.

Ans: EEG (electroencephalogram) is the recording of the electrical activity of the brain, taken by placing small metal discs called electrodes on the scalp; the recorded wave patterns show the electrical activity reflected from the cortex of the brain. ECG (electrocardiogram) is an electrical recording of the heart, made by recording the bio-electric currents generated by the heart through leads placed at specified locations on the body, and it is used in the investigation of heart diseases.

Q: 7. Why MRI is safer than CT scan?

Ans: A CT scan uses X-rays, which are ionizing radiations and can be harmful to the body. An MRI scan does not use X-rays; it produces its images with a strong magnetic field and radio waves, which do not carry this radiation harm. That is why MRI is safer than CT scan.

Q: 8. According to your opinion which technology has effected the human life a lot. Introduce this technology in few lines.

Ans: In my opinion computer technology has affected human life the most; the book itself calls it the most useful technology ever developed, and IT is the combination of computer technology and communications. A computer is an electronic device which processes the data entered into it and gives out the result rapidly, with high speed, accuracy and large memory. Computers provide a wide range of communication methods like email, social networks, chat, web and teleconferencing, and are used in education, business and industry.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Write in detail answers of the following questions

Q: 1. What are ultrasound waves? Why these waves are less harmful than X-rays.

Ans: The human ear can respond to sound having frequencies between 20 Hz and 20 KHz. Sound of frequency less than 20 Hz is called infrasonic and sound higher than 20 KHz is called ultrasonic. Ultrasound waves are longitudinal mechanical waves with frequency above the audible range, so they cannot be heard by the human ear, but they have greater penetrating power and are widely used as diagnostic, therapeutic and surgical tools in medicine and industry, for example to obtain cross-sectional pictures of a patient's organs and to examine the soft fleshy parts of the body. They are less harmful than X-rays because X-rays are electromagnetic radiations which ionize the atoms of the material they pass through, while ultrasonics are harmless mechanical sound waves which produce no after effects like X-rays or nuclear radiations; that is why ultrasonic scans are preferred to X-rays.

Q: 2. How CT scan has helped in providing better way of diagnosis and treatment of diseases?

Ans: Computerized tomography (CT) scans are a special type of X-ray test that produces cross-sectional images of the body using X-rays, the images being generated in the computer. With the help of CT scans, small nodules or tumors get detected which are not visible, unnoticed and undetected by ordinary X-rays, so such images help doctors to diagnose a certain abnormal condition developing in the body. CT scans are generally used to collect graphical information to assess the general health of the brain, neck, spine, chest, abdomen, pelvis and sinuses. An advantage of CT scan over other diagnostic procedures is that it is useful in the examination of soft body tissues like the liver, stomach and other abdominal organs; it is used for the examination of the brain to look for a mass, stroke, area of bleeding or blood vessel abnormality, as a confirmatory procedure for checking results already known from X-ray and ultrasound tests, and to see the spread of a cancer in the body — all of which leads to better and timely treatment.

Q: 3. Describe the principle of Lasers and its uses in different fields with examples.

Ans: Principle: Laser stands for 'light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation.' A laser is a device/source that produces an intense monochromatic and unidirectional coherent beam of visible light, and it operates by the principle of stimulated emission of a photon by an atom in excited state. A laser consists of two fundamental parts: (1) an amplifying medium, which can be solid, liquid or a gas and is composed of atoms, molecules, ions or electrons whose energy levels are used to increase the power of a light wave during its propagation; and (2) a pumping system, which excites the amplifying medium and creates the condition for light amplification — pumping can be optical, electrical or even chemical. Most lasers use a cavity or optical resonator with reflecting mirrors which bounce the light back and forth and amplify it considerably; the beam produced is pencil-sized and maintains its size and direction over very large distances. Uses: (1) telecommunications in space and open-air communications; (2) microsurgery of different body organs, e.g. thermal destruction of abnormal blood vessels of the eye; (3) bar-code scanners and printers for superior quality computer print outs; (4) industries, for boring and cutting metals and for cutting several layers of fabrics in the textile industry; (5) holography, generating a three-dimensional image of an object; (6) weapons like tanks, missiles and bombers, to locate the exact position of the enemy; and in everyday devices such as DVD and CD players.

Q: 4. Describe the functions and uses of ECG.

Ans: An electrocardiogram (ECG) is an electrical recording of the heart and is used in the investigation of heart disease; electrocardiography is the technique of recording the bio-electric currents generated by the heart. Cardiac muscle cells generate bio-currents which can be detected inside the body or on its surface using special electrodes; unlike the bio-currents of other muscles, the currents generated by the heart muscles are periodic, consisting of a repeated sequence of characteristic waveforms which correspond to a heart beat. An electrocardiographic lead is a recording electrode or a pair of recording electrodes at a specified location on the body; in clinical practice twelve leads are usually used in the diagnostic ECG, and the leads are usually placed on the elbows and stifles (knees). The graphical display of this recording is called the electrocardiogram. For more than one hundred years the ECG has been used to reveal the condition of the heart and to diagnose cardiac illnesses.

Q: 5. Describe the functions and uses of EEG.

Ans: The electroencephalogram (EEG) is a diagnostic procedure in which the electrical activity of the brain is recorded by placing small metal discs called electrodes on the scalp. The brain is composed of nerve cells or neurons which produce electrical signals known as action potentials, and the recorded waves form patterns which show the electrical activity reflected from the cortex of the brain — the largest part of the brain, concerned with higher functions such as thought and action. For taking the reading, electrodes are placed on the scalp at specific positions, each site labelled with a letter referring to the area of brain underlying it (e.g. T–Temporal lobe, F–Frontal lobe) and a number; the electrodes are connected with wires to an instrument that amplifies the brain waves and records them on computer equipment. During the test the technician may ask the patient to open and close the eyes, perform simple calculations, read a paragraph, look at a picture or a flashing light, or breathe deeply; video is frequently recorded at the same time, and this combined recording of body motions and brain waves may help the doctor diagnose and treat a medical problem.

Q: 6. Describe the main components of a computer.

Ans: A computer system is composed of different components which work in a coordinated fashion for the accomplishment of a certain task; overall, a computer has a hardware component (the parts which can be touched and are visible to the eyes) and a software component (the programmes and applications that direct the hardware for effective functioning). The major parts are: (i) Central Processing Unit (CPU) — it executes the instructions sequentially; the instructions modify data stored in memory or obtained from an input device, and the CPU contains the Control Unit and the Arithmetic Logic Unit. (ii) Memory or storage — electronic data is stored in the memory, from where it is processed as and where instructed; there are two types, primary storage (ROM, the permanent memory supplied by the manufacturer, and RAM, the temporary memory) and secondary storage (USB, memory cards, etc.), which gives backup storage and increases the data storage capacity. (iii) Input Units — an input device is any hardware component that allows a user to enter data and instructions into a computer, e.g. mouse, keyboard, microphone, digital camera and scanners. (iv) Output Units — an output device communicates the results of data processing to the user, e.g. monitor, printers and computer speakers; results can be viewed on the screen or printed by the printer for permanent record.

Q: 7. Explain the contribution SUPARCO has made in the development of our country and list their future plans.

Ans: SUPARCO means 'Pakistan Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission'; it was established in 1962 and is responsible for the execution of the space science and technology programmes in the country. It prepares and submits proposals, schemes and projects to the Government of Pakistan, carries out approved research and application programmes, conducts investigations and surveys related to space and the upper atmosphere, and works through its divisions — Remote Sensing and Application (satellite remote sensing data, GIS technology for exploring earth resources, surveying, mapping and environmental monitoring), Environmental and Space Science, Ionosphere Research, and Satellite Communications. Contribution: this research centre sent several satellites for weather research — the first satellite Badar-I was sent into space in 1990, after which Badar-II was sent; Pakistan has its own communication satellite responsible for communication all over the country, its own surveillance satellite which can check each and every movement in the region, and a monsoon watch programme whose weather satellite successfully predicts information about rain, storms and hurricanes. Future plans: Pakistan's National Satellite Development Programme (NSDP) is a major task entrusted to SUPARCO, including the development of an effective communication satellite, the Pakistan Remote Sensing Satellite (PRSS-1), and human resource development in the area of space exploration; in Applications Programmes the fields focused for further studies are Remote Sensing Applications, Space and Atmospheric Sciences, and Tele-Medicine.

Q: 8. Write a note on the working of a telephone.

Ans: The word tele means far or distance and phone means sound, so telephone means something that lets you hear sound from a distance. A telephone has two main parts. (1) Speaker (transmitter): most telephones use a carbon powder speaker transmitter, a device to turn the sound wave into electric signals; the carbon powder is present in a case, and when we speak, the sound vibrates the plastic membrane and presses the carbon powder — the resistance of the powder drops when it is under pressure, so the sound vibration changes the electric current correspondingly. (2) Receiver: the receiver turns the incoming signals into sound; as the signals pass through the electromagnet, it attracts the thin metal membrane, the changes in the amplitude of the signals vary the attraction and cause the membrane to vibrate accordingly, and this vibration is transmitted in the air as sound waves, so we can hear the sound. In short, when we speak on the telephone, the sound energy changes into electrical signals; these signals travel along the telephone cable and the receiver on the other end changes them again into sound. In the latest technology the electrical signals are converted into light signals which travel along optical fibers, so several thousand calls can be transmitted through a single optical fiber at the same time with no interference from electric or magnetic fields.

Q: 9. What is the role of information technology in our society? How it has revolutionized the human life?

Ans: The rapid advancements in electronics have provided new tools such as television, computer, internet, telephone and satellites, and our society is changing due to developments in information technology. IT is based on the hardware and software of a computer and the telecommunication infrastructure, and IT is the combination of computer technology and communications; computer technology is the most useful technology ever developed, and computers are becoming more and more powerful in computational speed and data storage capacity. The methods used in sending information instantly over long distances are called telecommunications, the devices being television, computer, radio, telephones and fax machines. In education, the computer provides an efficient mechanism for storage of and access to information and preserves data for future use, and online education has made distance learning a reality; in business, ordering products, shipping information and price checks in retail stores are done using computers, and accounting software ensures the accuracy of financial status; in manufacturing industry computers are widely used to design and manufacture products; and computers provide a wide range of communication methods like email, social networks, chat, web and teleconferencing. In this way information technology has revolutionized human life, making information, communication, learning and business instant and worldwide.
